content: Linear atrophoderma of Moulin (LAM) is an acquired dermatological condition characterized by unilateral hyperpigmented dermatitis that follows the lines of Blaschko. This condition was first described in 1992 by Dr. Moulin, after whom it was initially named atrophoderma of Moulin. It was later renamed as linear atrophoderma of Moulin. LAM represents a cutaneous manifestation of mosaicism, a phenomenon where two or more genetically distinct cell populations exist within an individual. The differential diagnosis of LAM includes other linear dermatoses, such as: Blaschkitis acuta Epidermal naevi Inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal naevus Lichen striatus Linear lupus erythematosus Linear scleroderma Reticulate hyperpigmentation of Iijima Only a few dozen cases of LAM have been documented in the medical literature. It predominantly affects children or adolescents of both genders. The natural history of LAM is notable for the absence of preceding inflammation, as well as the lack of subsequent induration or scleroderma. While the condition can be disfiguring, potentially leading to emotional distress, the overall prognosis is favorable. On physical examination, the rash typically involves the trunk and limbs. The clinical diagnosis is supported by findings from microscopic pathology. In terms of treatment, intravenous penicillin G has been used historically. The recommended regimen involved administering 10 x 10^6 IU twice daily for a duration of 14 days.
